questions.q: Per this lesson, why do real Salesforce development teams avoid building code-heavy work directly in a shared sandbox?
options: A shared sandbox has no reliable change history, no clean way to discard risky work, and no gate against broken code landing where the team depends on it
Sandboxes cannot run Apex code at all
Sandboxes are more expensive than scratch orgs
Sandboxes cannot contain custom objects
questions.explain: The lesson gives these specific reasons for source-driven development with scratch orgs instead of building directly in a shared sandbox.

questions.q: Which command style does this lesson say is current for the Salesforce CLI, and which is deprecated?
options: `sfdx force:org:create` is current; `sf org create scratch` is deprecated
Both command styles were retired in favor of a GUI-only tool
`sf` commands (e.g. `sf org create scratch`) are current; the older `sfdx`-prefixed commands are deprecated
Neither style exists; Salesforce CLI uses only REST calls
questions.explain: The lesson states the sf command set is current, while the older sfdx-prefixed style (like sfdx force:org:create) is deprecated and being phased out.

questions.q: What does the scratch org definition file (`project-scratch-def.json`) control?
options: The Git commit history for the project
The list of Apex test classes to run
The REST endpoint used for the warranty claim integration
Which Salesforce edition and features a freshly created scratch org should have
questions.explain: The scratch org definition file specifies the edition, license types, and org preferences so every scratch org created from it is identically configured.

questions.q: In this capstone's workflow, where does the lesson say the real source of truth for metadata lives?
options: In the scratch org itself, since it is always available
In the Git repository, with the scratch org treated as disposable
In a shared spreadsheet maintained by Jules
In Salesforce's production org directly
questions.explain: Because a scratch org is disposable, the lesson treats the Git repository as the source of truth, pulling any declarative changes back into local files to make them 'real.'

questions.q: Which command does this lesson give for pulling declarative changes made in a scratch org's Setup UI back into local project files?
options: `sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app`
`sf org open`
`sf project retrieve start --source-dir force-app`
`git commit -m "sync"`
questions.explain: sf project retrieve start pulls metadata changes made in the org back down into the local force-app source directory.
